transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-22 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Maya (Catalyst Head of ML), Omar (CTO), Rachel (Infra)

Summary (auto): discuss per-token pricing, batching/caching, dedicated commit math, security and benchmarks.

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, excited to dig into the cost side — we know that's top of mind. Quick intros?
[00:18] Maya: Hi yeah Maya here, we run conversational flows across finance ops, we have lots of short queries but also some long context threads so cost per token matters.
[00:25] Omar: Omar here, CTO, I'm mostly worried about TCO and whether we need a dedicated pool.
[00:30] Rachel: Rachel — infra, will own network/KMS.
[00:35] Samir: Samir, SE at Redwood, I'll cover batching/kv caching details and benchmarks.
[00:42] Avery: Cool. So two broad options we see — Hosted for quick start, Dedicated for predictable unit economics and traffic isolation, Private/VPC if you need network controls.
[01:05] Maya: Quick question — what's our ballpark per-token on hosted, and how does batching change that?
[01:12] Avery: Right, so for hosted generation we show example pricing in the model catalog — ballpark for a Llama-2-ish-sized model is about $0.004 per 1k tokens for generation, embeddings lower — but key is effective cost after batching and cache. With batching and prefix KV caching you can reduce token compute by up to 30-60% depending on reuse.
[01:38] Omar: Wait, 0.004 per 1k? That seems high compared to some providers — is that list or with discounts?
[01:45] Avery: It's a public example list price; committed Dedicated pools can drop effective per-token substantially — we can run the numbers: a monthly reserved commit with 8x GPUs can push per-token to sub-$0.0015 in many workloads, especially with aggressive batching.
[02:05] Maya: How realistic is that for our workload? We have many short-turn requests, low reuse.
[02:12] Samir: Short requests reduce batching benefit but KV cache helps if users have repeated prefixes or system prompts. For pure short-turn, batching at the network layer still helps — continuous batching groups requests arriving within the scheduling window. You trade a few ms latency for better throughput.
[02:30] [02:30] Maya: Is there a chart or sample math you can send?
[02:33] Avery: Yes — I'll send a cost model spreadsheet that takes your QPS, avg tokens in and out, hit-rate assumptions for cache, and shows hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[02:40] Omar: On latency — we need 95th pct under 400ms for short queries, can dedicated help?
[02:46] Samir: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower queue latencies; you can configure warm pools and autoscale policies. For sub-400ms you'll want to pin lower batch windows and ensure model variants with faster kernels.
[03:05] Maya: Security wise Rachel will want SOC2 and KMS — is that available for hosted?
[03:12] Avery: Hosted has enterprise plans with SOC2 reports, customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private, and audit logs. For Private deployments you can bring your own HSM. I'll share the SOC2 pack.
[03:28] Rachel: Good. Also data residency — can we guarantee EU-only?
[03:33] Avery: Yes, we can route to region-specific capacity; Dedicated or Private gives more control.
[03:40] Omar: Back to cost — what's the biggest lever we can control quickly?
[03:44] Samir: There are three levers: batching (reduce per-token compute by packing sequences), KV/prefix caching (avoid re-decoding tokens for repeated context), and quantized model variants (reduce GPU cost per token). Also routing to cheaper model variants for non-critical queries helps.
[04:05] Maya: Can you quantify e.g., if we have 200k tokens/day, what we save?
[04:10] Samir: With intelligent batching + 40% KV hit-rate, you might cut compute tokens by ~35% leading to ~30% cost reduction; on Dedicated the percent savings amplify because base per-token compute is already lower.
[04:25] Omar: Example: hosted is list $0.004/1k, with 30% reduction that's ~0.0028/1k, but Dedicated might start at 0.0016/1k and fall to 0.0011/1k after optimizations — rough numbers.
[04:43] Maya: That helps, thanks. What's the minimum commit for Dedicated?
[04:48] Avery: Typical entry is a monthly reserved pool equivalent to a few p3d-style GPUs, but we size based on your throughput. We can show a 3-tier commit model in the spreadsheet: small, medium, large.
[05:00] Rachel: For private, do we still get Redwood console observability?
[05:04] Samir: Yes, Private includes the console and telemetry, with logs sent to your VPC.
[05:10] Omar: Are there any gotchas with batching and real-time UX? If we increase batch window we may add latency spikes.
[05:16] Samir: Exactly — it's a balance. You tune batch delay (ms) and max batch size; for a conversational UX we usually target batch windows under 50ms for low-latency, heavier batching for throughput at cost of a small latency increase. Also continuous batching avoids big tail spikes.
[05:36] [05:36] Maya: Do you support model quantization workflows? We run LLMs in int8 sometimes.
[05:40] Samir: Yes, we support quantized model variants; our runtime picks kernels and quantization-friendly paths. That reduces memory and increases concurrency per GPU so lower $/token. We'll note which open models are verified.
[05:54] Omar: What about failover — if Dedicated capacity saturates, does Redwood fallback to hosted?
[05:59] Avery: Yes, smart routing supports fallbacks by policy; you can prefer dedicated but fallback to hosted-compatible variants with rate limits so you don't drop requests.
[06:10] Maya: Can we run a benchmark with our traces?
[06:12] Samir: Absolutely. If you drop sample traces (anonymized) we'll run the throughput and latency tests and return a CSV with tokens/sec, latency distributions, and cost per 1k tokens under different configs.
[06:25] Rachel: We need to anonymize — is that fine?
[06:28] Samir: Totally fine — we don't need PII. Just the tokenized traces or representative prompts and response lengths.
[06:34] Omar: Pricing—are there scaling discounts as usage grows?
[06:36] Avery: Yes, usage-based hosted has tiered discounts and enterprise commit discounts; Dedicated comes with committed capacity pricing and volume credits. We'll show examples in the model.
[06:48] Maya: What's the expected time to spin up a dedicated pool?
[06:51] Avery: Typically 2-4 weeks for an initial pool for enterprise customers (depending on region/hardware), hosted is instant. For Private/on-prem it depends on your infra and network, usually 4-8 weeks.
[07:05] Omar: Can you summarize recommended next steps?
[07:08] Avery: Sure — we propose: 1) Catalyst provide 7 days of anonymized traces, 2) Redwood runs benchmark and returns cost/perf CSV, 3) Redwood sends tailored cost spreadsheet and SOC2/KMS docs, 4) follow-up meeting to review.
[07:26] Maya: Works for us.
[07:28] [07:28] Interrupt — brief noise, sorry.
[07:35] Samir: one more note on caching — for chat, if you keep a per-user cache we can store KV cache across sessions to avoid recompute for repeated system prompts; that can be huge for certain flows.
[07:52] Maya: We do some reuse but not a ton, we'll include metrics.
[07:56] Omar: Any concerns around model drift and quality when using cheaper variants?
[08:00] Samir: Yes quality tradeoffs exist; Redwood Optimize can run evals and regression alerts across prompt sets so you can route lower-cost variants for non-critical flows only.
[08:12] Maya: How do we measure end-to-end cost including networking, storage?
[08:16] Avery: The spreadsheet includes a section for infra adders — data egress, storage of logs, snapshot costs; for Private you account for your own infra. We'll add a sample breakout.
[08:30] Rachel: Is there an SLA for Hosted?
[08:33] Avery: Hosted has best-effort for self-serve; enterprise-hosted and Dedicated have SLA tiers — we'll include SLA language.
[08:40] Omar: Ok good. Any security red flags?
[08:44] Rachel: I want to confirm key rotation cadence and whether logs expose tokens — we can't store PII in logs.
[08:49] Samir: We support redaction and never store full user tokens in logs unless configured; KMS integrates and keys can be rotated per your policy. We'll include the config docs.
[09:02] Maya: Great.
[09:05] Avery: Next steps recap — send spreadsheet, run benchmark, share SOC2/KMS docs, schedule follow-up.
[09:12] Omar: Thanks all.
[09:15] [09:15] Call transitions to scheduling details, then off-line chat.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-IDs and filler.

End of transcript.
